lessons.title: Section 1: "Nothing I Knit Fits!" ... Consider This:

components.html:
Welcome!

A knitter recently shared with me me how disappointed she was with her knitting machine because "nothing fits". 
This entire course is a result of my trying to convince her that her machine isn't the issue ... it's patterns!

Our goal is to get your brain cells working and spark your creativity. It's up to you to learn how to knit sweaters that fit.

Don't just follow knitting patterns and hope that the designer had your body in mind when they did the math!

blocks.title: Can You Relate to This Knitter?

components.html:
All knitting patterns use generic sizing charts. It’s up to you to learn how to adapt them to yourself and your preferences.
I like ease in my sweaters (I pretend that it covers up the lumps and bumps).
My slim daughter-in-law likes to show off her curves.  We may have the same bust size, but she has a great figure and likes less ease.

NO ready-made knitting pattern is going to give both of us the results we want.

Knit it Now Patterns use one set of sizing charts. Other designers use different charts. It's CRITICAL for you to examine the dimensions before you start knitting.
Knit it Now Sizing Charts display body dimensions. (no ease)

Focus on one machine

Do you have more than one knitting machine?  Which is your favorite? Perhaps it’s the gauge and the and the electronics.  Maybe you LOVE your punchcard machine.
No matter the reason, mastering ONE  machine will go a long way towards knitting sweaters that fit.
Why?  If you aren’t burdened with figuring out which buttons to push, you’ll be able to focus on techniques that will add to your satisfaction with your finished item.

Best advice … put all but one machine away for a while and focus on your favorite.

Use the same yarn for a while

If you are a sewist, you probably wouldn’t use the same sewing pattern with denim and with a knit. Each has its own properties.
The same for yarn.  Take a natural fiber. Knit 2 swatches.  Let one rest and wet block the other.  When you measure for gauge, you’ll get very different numbers.  If your swatches have any man-made fiber content, hit one with steam and compare …. Lots of variables, with one yarn.
Switch to a different yarn and do the same thing.  The differences may be even greater.
The point is, each yarn has its own characteristics.  Once you learn the “personality” of a particular yarn, stick with it. I know a professional designer who only uses one yarn.  She knits hundreds of custom designer garments.
When she knits a sleeve, she KNOWS what size it is going to be.  This also allows her to get creative.  She can play with color, she can make colorblock pieces … plus she KNOWS that the sweater is going to fit!

Swatch

At the risk of sounding like a broken record “Swatching is NOT optional”.

If you are working with the same yarn every time and you have an accurate gauge swatch you won’t be surprised by the size of a finished piece.

BUT .. one thing to consider is “drop”. Knitters often will knit a 6” square for a gauge swatch.  We then knit a garment back that is 23” long.  We put in on our body and we’re surprised that it’s too long.  Maybe it hugs around the body because the weight of the yarn is narrowing the garment piece.

Knit large swatches, let them hang AND measure them hanging.  This is especially true for lace and some openwork stitch patterns. (You aren't wasting yarn ... how much yarn will be wasted on a sweater that doesn't fit and won't be worn?)

We will talk more about swatching and gauge and offer some practice exercises further along in the course.

Knit in one stitch pattern until you gain experience and confidence

As tempting as it is, don’t play with stitch patterning until you establish a good fit for you.

For example, tuck and lace knit up very differently than stockinette. They will hang on the body differently as well, affecting fit. Once you find a pattern that you love, it may not “translate” well to a different stitch pattern.  Think of denim and knit fabric.  You probably wouldn’t sew a t-shirt with bottom-weight denim.

Yes, as knitters we can successfully substitute stitch patterns, but until you establish YOUR fit style, you will be frustrated.  Unlike fabric, when we start out we don’t have yards of fabric to touch, feel and observe the drape.  It’s not until we’ve used the yarn and stitch pattern for a while that we can KNOW the end result BEFORE knitting.

components.title: Another rant ... but this is important!

components.html:
Read a pattern completely before starting to knit


Why would you knit an entire sweater before knowing exactly the sleeve length or the depth of the armhole?
Hopefully you wouldn’t purchase a garment online without at AT LEAST checking the sizing chart.
Starting to knit without knowing what the designer had in mind is just plain silly! My idea of a "comfy" fit is a lot different than my daughter-in-law.
In addition to fit, don't you want to know (and practice) knitting techniques BEFORE you use that beautiful, expensive garment yarn?
Read (and understand) the pattern completely before starting to knit.

If your pattern doesn't have a diagram, you'll need to create one before you start knitting. We will learn to do this down the road in this course.

Find/measure a sweater that you LOVE

Why measure your body?

Look in your closet. If you have a sweater that you love, start there. It may take a shopping trip to find the perfect sweater. 

Another option is to determine what you DON'T like about garments you own. Love that sweater, but the sleeves are too long? Measure them! Love the length of that woven jacket? Measure it!

  1. Take a pen and paper and a TAPE MEASURE with you to document what you like. 
  2. Measure every inch of the sweater.
  3. Record the length, record the armhole depth, record the sleeve length, record the neck depth.
  4.  Make notes about WHY you like this sweater.


We will walk through measuring a sample sweater later in the course

Arm yourself with knowledge BEFORE you start to knit.

In this course we will discuss methods of adjusting knitting patterns to fit YOU! Use whatever method makes sense to you ... combine techniques!

  1. Use software to chart your own sweater pattern (DesignaKnit, Garment Designer etc)

  2. Modify an existing pattern based on your personal fit (Knit it Now Dynamic patterns or any pattern)

    • Use Basic Math
    • Use the Knit it Now Tools

  3. Use a charting device (Knit Leader - Knit Radar)
Is there math in involved?  A bit … but nothing that a 5th grader can’t do.   Honestly, I’m math -challenged and I can do this … so can you!

blocks.title: The Secret to Obtaining Good Fit

components.html:
What's the biggest issue? Over all size of the sweater? Bust? Shoulders? Sleeve Length?
Let's not get hung up on measurements for now. Just identify what you see as your issues.

Let's face it, our knitting machines were designed when people were much smaller than they are today. Many knitters find that they don't have enough needles on the needlebed to knit the width they need.

We have to get creative.

Have you ever looked at a vintage Japanese machine knitting magazine or book? Notice that the patterns are all in diagram format ... but in only 1 or 2 sizes!

Were all Japanese ladies of that time the same size?

Let's face it, our knitting machines were designed when people were much smaller than they are today. Many knitters find that they don't have enough needles on the needlebed to knit the width they need.
We have to get creative.

Have you ever looked at a vintage Japanese machine knitting magazine or book? Notice that the patterns are all in diagram format ... but in only 1 or 2 sizes!
Were all Japanese ladies of that time the same size?

Sizing and Ease: (we are all different)
  • Some like it hot (no ease)
  • Some like it cold (roomy)
  • Some like it just right (It's your choice!)
When choosing a size to knit with any knitting pattern, choose based on the finished garment size.
With Knit it Now Dynamic patterns, on the build page of the pattern (where you enter your gauge and select the size) is an interactive chart that shows the finished garment size.  Measure a sweater that you like to determine how much ease you want in your sweater. Chose your size based on the finished size.
Measure something you love
and copy it!

lessons.title: Section 3: Your Success Depends on This

components.html:
These concepts are so important that they are worth repeating.
  1. Decide on ONE machine for the next few projects. Get to know (and master) this machine. Understand its quirks and personality.
  2. Decide on ONE yarn type for the next few projects.
  • Determine the gauge in ONE stitch pattern. Use it again and again.
  • Learn how the yarn knits. Does it have knots to watch for? Are there plys that can be problematic if you have to rip rows?
  • Learn how the knitting washes and wears. Give your swatch the "throw it in the wash with jeans" test and see what happens.
  • Is the color and fiber something you would wear? Don't spend time perfecting the fit of your sweater with junk yarn in a terrible color that you won't enjoy working with or wearing.
  1. To test the wearability, washability, and workability of a yarn, knit a small blanket using your chosen yarn and stitch pattern. You can always donate it to your local animal shelter as a "blankie" for a pet looking for a home.
Before even thinking about knitting a sweater, get experience with your chosen yarn. Once you create a "blueprint" of your perfect sweater, you can experiment with different yarns. Why complicate the fitting process by introducing all the variables that different yarns and stitch patterns bring?

We spend a lot of time planning, practicing and thinking about knitting. We spend money on yarn and patterns. Even though machine knitting is fast, we all have limited time to devote to knitting.
Why invest all that time, money and energy and not be happy with the results? The ONLY WAY to ensure success is to establish correct gauge.
DON'T SKIP THIS SECTION!
Your success with this course AND your success with your knitting machine depends on your understanding and mastering the art of knitting gauge swatches.
Without a swatch we are knitting in the dark.
  • Is it going to fit?
  • How is the final sweater going to feel in the yarn and stitch pattern you've chosen?
  • Do you have enough yarn?
  • Do you have enough needles on your machine for the size you chose?

SWATCHING IS NOT OPTIONAL

Let's double check your gauge ... let's MAKE SURE you are on track, before you start knitting another sweater.
We won't bore you with instruction for knitting gauge swatches. Your manual will give you good instructions for the mechanics of knitting a swatch.
The important thing for this course is MEASURING GAUGE (accurately)
Optional caption or notes.
Optional caption or notes.
Optional text below the videos. Summarize key points, compare techniques, or provide an exercise/challenge.

If you haven't used your chosen yarn before, how do you know the best tension to knit your sweater?
  Knitters tend to use the terms "tension swatch" and "gauge swatch" interchangeably, lets take a look at both.

GAUGE SWATCH

The gauge swatch is the "official" swatch used when designing a garment.
It is knit at a specific size, marked for accurate stitch and row measurement and "dressed" as the final garment will be treated.
TIP: Whatever method you use to create a swatch, the key is to correctly measure it and calculate your gauge.

TENSION SWATCH

(Getting-to-Know-You Swatch)
When I pick up a new cone of yarn, I can't wait to thread up my machine and see what the yarn looks like.   From the initial cast on, I start guessing what setting on my tension dial I need to use.  I knit a few inches and reach down and start to feel the resulting fabric.
 
Once I get a feel for the yarn (what machine, general tension setting at stockinette, etc) I create a Tension Swatch (Get Acquainted).  This helps me fine-tune the tension needed to achieve the fabric I like and allows me to play with various techniques.  I'm often very surprised that a yarn looks great in tuck, and awful in slip, for example.  Adding a few eyelets here and there tells me if the yarn will work up in lace.

Let's practice knitting a Getting-to-Know-You or tension swatch.

Try it yourself
  1. Play!
  2. Start knitting stockenette at the tightest tension that will knit.  (If the tension is too tight, you'll see stitches that don't form properly.
  3. Knit 2-4 inches. Knit a marker row (change colors, work a few eyelets across the row or knit a sewing thread in with the main yarn)
  4. Keep knitting sections, marking the tension dial number in each section.  Knit the last section as loosely as possiblle, even if you think this will be too loose ... I'm often very pleasantly surprised at the result.
  5. Transfer every other needle to out of work postion and knit a section - put all needles back into work.
  6. Work a simple tuck, or slip, or any stitch pattern of your choice ... base your tension dial setting on the stockinette sections you just knit.
The point of this exercise is to put the yarn through it's paces ... ignite your creativity, and get a feel for what the yarn can do.  If you don't have a huge cone, you can always re-wind this knitting. At this point, you probably know exactly what you want to do with this yarn.  Knit your Gauge Swatch, dress it and and you are ready to design and knit your sweater.

components.introHtml:
Things to consider when measuring
  • Rest and dress your swatch before measuring
  • These swatches are flat ... probably not the most accurate for larger pieces. You will want to hang your swatch (and possibly add a bit of weight) to account for drop
  • Most hand knitters think we are crazy to calculate out 2 decimal places. Is "close enough" good enough for you? This is knitting after all
  • These swatches are both the same number of stitches and rows. Don't forget to swatch for each stitch pattern you will be using, including combinations of stitch patterns within a piece

components.html:
There are many ways to knit a gauge swatch. At this point you probably have your favorite method. Work the next 2 exercises with whatever method you prefer.
The method used isn't as important as learning to measure accurately.
Time to get knitting!
  1. Knit a swatch using any method.
  2. Place markers at the center of the swatch as you did with the previous swatch
  3. Let it rest
  4. Dress the swatch (treat it as you will treat your finished sweater)
  5. Accurately measure YOUR stitch and row gauge LAYING FLAT
  6. Accurately measure YOUR stitch and row gauge AFTER HANGING
  7. Record your gauge.

Does your swatch look similar to this one?
Attach a string tag to your swatch recording all the details ... it's funny how easy it is to forget. Include yarn name, machine, tension, measurements, and stitch pattern number (if appropriate)
To hang your swatch: Insert a blocking wire or a straight hand knitting along the cast on or bind off edge of the swatch. Pin it to a corkboard or clip it in a skirt hanger and hang in a doorway.

Please take time to knit this swatch ... you may be surprised at the difference between the swatches with your yarn and your stitch pattern.

Compare using a larger swatch using the same yarn

  1. Knit a LARGE swatch using any method.
  2. Place markers at the center of the swatch as you did with the previous swatch (measure the same number of stitches and rows)
  3. Let it rest
  4. Dress the swatch (treat it as you will treat your finished sweater)
  5. Accurately measure YOUR stitch and row gauge
  6. Record your gauge and compare to swatch 1

Knit at least 100 sts x 100 rows for a standard gauge machine and 50 sts x 50 rows for bulky. The point is to duplicate the weight of a larger piece and examine the impact on gauge.

Print the Worksheet to follow along

Let's use this pattern to practice creating a schematic/diagram from a hand knitting pattern.
This is the basic shape of the sample sweater - it's long-sleeved, drop shoulder with a small funnel neck collar.
Next we will start filling in the blanks based on the written pattern.
The Designer gave us these 3 finished measurements and we've filled them in on our worksheet

Your Turn!

Uncover the stitches and row instructions for the sleeves.

Using your Worksheet and the Original Pattern do the math to calculate the stitches and rows for the sleeves.

Remember the 1" and 1 cm stitch and row multipliers that we established earlier.

4" / 10 cm 1 inch 1 cm
13 sts 3.25 sts 1.3 sts
18 rows 4.5 rows 1.8 rows

You are ready to knit this sweater if:

  • You can match the designer's gauge
  • You can wear this size
Coming up .... we'll discuss some alternative ways of using this hand knitting pattern on the machine.

slides.caption:
The drop shoulder sweater is the easiest and fastest style to knit. With minimal shaping, it's often recommended for beginner knitters. It's perfect if you are doing a lot of hand manipulation, adding complicated stitch patterns or color work, or using the g-carriage.
This style is very common in ready-to-wear because it can easily fit a wide range of sizes.

Square armhole is also called "modified drop shoulder" shaping. Again, there is minimal shaping, that makes for easy knitting. Because the sleeve seams are higher on the shoulders, this style can be more flattering, but still fit a range of sizes and body types.
Notice the bind off edges at the underarms and the matching straight knitting on the sleeves. This makes it a bit more difficult to set in the sleeve, but nothing you can't master.

A variation on the Square armhole is the Full Fashioned sleeve.  Notice the diagonal shaping at the underarm.  This provides a better fit with less bulk at the underarm. Simple decreases create the shaping on both body and sleeve.

The classic set in sleeve has shaped armholes and a shaped sleeve cap. This is a very popular and flattering style for all figures.
BUT it has the most shaping. If you are short on time, or just getting started with your machine, you may want to consider another style.
This style of sleeve isn't hard to knit, it just takes more time and knitting experience. Knit it Now offers a complete course "Set in Sleeve Perfection" to help you master this style with practice BEFORE you start knitting your perfect sweater .

components.introHtml:
The secret to knitting your PERFECT sweater is to identify what you want.
Would you blindly follow a recipe without checking out the ingredients? Maybe you HATE turnips. If a recipe calls for turnips, you will probably eliminate or substitute something else.
No knitting pattern written by someone else will ever be PERFECT for YOU!

Let's look at 4 basic sweater styles. Your favorite may be styled a little differently, but we'll use these basic shapes to establish measurement. We'll address styling later.

components.html:
Everyone has a favorite T-shirt or sweatshirt that just feels right. If you wanted another one to fit exactly the same, would you measure yourself? Of course not. You'd measure the shirt.
INSTEAD OF MAKING A PATTERN FIT OUR DIMENSIONS, LETS DETERMINE A COMFORTABLE SIZE FOR OUR SWEATER AND KNIT THE SWEATER TO THOSE DIMENSIONS!

Up next:

The secret to custom fit ... copy the packaging that fits YOU!

blocks.title: Create the Vest with a Charting Device

components.html:
If you use DesignaKnit, please don't skip this tutorial.

This exercise may seem a little silly because DAK has Standard Garment Shaping built in. But the skills presented will go a long way towards creating more complex garment shapes.
The concept of using ZERO EASE to duplicate the vest may be new to you. All of the edits are done in Standard Garment Shaping only.

Your Turn!

Uncover the stitch and row instructions for the sleeves.

Using your Worksheet and the original pattern, calculate the sleeve instructions.

Work out:

  • Cast-on stitches
  • Increase frequency
  • Total sleeve rows
  • Final stitch count before binding off

Compare your answers to the worksheet before moving on.

You are ready to knit this sweater when:

  • You can match the designer's gauge.
  • The finished size will fit the intended wearer.
  • You have completed the sleeve calculations.

Next, we'll look at a few alternative ways to adapt this hand-knitting pattern for your knitting machine.

We explored 3 methods of creating Walt's Sweater
  1. Convert a Hand Knitting Pattern with math and Knit it Now Tools

  2. Use a Charting Device

  3. Use DesignaKnit or other software

No matter what shape of sleeve, you don't need to settle for sleeves being too long or too short. Determine your perfect length and adjust your pattern accordingly.
Lets explore different methods for adjusting your sleeve length.
The Tools have been updated - Find the new Magic Formula Tool here

Using a Charting Device is probably the easiest way to adjust your sleeve length ... just draw the sleeve to the correct size at scale.
TIP: Once you establish your sleeve cap, draw multiple sleeve lengths and styles on the same mylar. Mark each style with a different color to make it easier to follow as you knit.
If you find you are tugging down on the front or back of your sweaters, consider adjusting the length.
Men, women, new mammas can need additional length in front

Most knitting patterns do not include bust darts. Many knitters simply rely on the stretch of the knitted fabric.
BUT . . . Simply adding a few rows of knitting to the center front of your sweaters will add comfort and allow your sweaters to hang parallel to the floor.
Unlike adding rows for a rounded back or tummy, darts are positioned to point to the fullest part of the bust, adding length and shape to a sweater.

Use the tabs below to explore different methods for adding bust darts.
  • Knit it Now Patterns
  • Commercial Patterns + Math
  • Charting Device
  • DesignaKnit
Knit it Now Dynamic Patterns include a link to a tool to help you add bust darts. Watch how it's done.
Use the Knit it Now Tool to calculate your Bust Dart Shaping
Add bust dart shaping to your mylar to be used with a charting device.
  1. Draw the front piece as desired (without darts)
  2. Determine the positioning and depth of your dart
  3. Add the dart to the mylar (just draw a line)
  4. When you reach the start of the dart, note the row counter
  5. Use the Knit it Now Dart Tool (the magic formula or graph paper) to determine the knitting instructions
  6. Pause the charting device
  7. Work the dart(s) with short row shaping
  8. Finish by knitting 1 row across all held needles
  9. RESET YOUR ROW COUNTER to the count before starting the dart
  10. Continue knitting the front
NOTE: Remember you are adding length (rows) to the center of the front piece, but not to the side seams. When done, the row counter should match the row count for the back of your knitting.

Explore 2 methods of using DAK to create bust darts.

This topic falls more into the "Design Element" category than fit. Some patterns are designed with very wide necklines. Have you ever had a top that felt like it was falling off your shoulders? Unless you have a collar or other design element around the neckline, you don't have to completely re-chart the neckline. Just one small change can make a huge difference.

Check the pattern for the neck opening width to determine if you want to make a change.
This pattern for a round neckline is instructing us to bind off 32 stitches at the center front. Looking at the diagram (or doing the math) I've determined that I want the neck opening to be 2" narrower.

Instead of making big pattern changes:
  1. Bind off fewer stitches at the center front
  2. Continue following the pattern and work the neckline shaping as instructed
  3. You will have more stitches at the shoulder seams
  4. The neck opening will be narrower
  5. Don't forget to repeat this on the back as well, so the shoulders match
Read the pattern or use a diagram to establish the neck opening width in the pattern. Determine if you want to make a change.

Written Patterns:
  • Use the armhole and sleeve from a larger size. Knit the garment to the armhole opening, then use the larger size instructions for the armhole. Knit the neckline shaping according to the original size.
Charting Device:
  • Adjust the upper arm, sleeve cap and armhole
DesignaKnit:
  • Set the upper arm measurement in Standard Garment Styling and DAK will accurately adjust the sleeve, sleeve head and armohole.

Use the tabs below to explore different methods for adding shaped shoulders.
  • Knit it Now Patterns
  • Commercial Patterns + Math
  • Charting Device
  • DesignaKnit

Knit it Now Dynamic Patterns offer shaped shoulder versions. If you need more shaping, think of the armhole as a block of instructions to be adjusted without changing the depth of the armhole or impacting the fit of the sleeves. Use the Magic Formula to calculate the shoulder shaping.

To add shoulder shaping to a commercial pattern, think of the armhole as a block of instructions to be adjusted without changing the depth of the armhole or impacting the fit of the sleeves.Use the Magic Formula to accurately calculate the shaping.

Using a Charting Device is probably the easiest way to add shaped shoulders ... just be sure that the armhole opening and sleeve cap match!


Explore a couple of methods of using DAK to adjust your sleeve length.

Armholes that are too deep or shallow can cause many fit issues. Examine your favorite sweater to determine the depth of the armhole.
Because the sleeve cap must match the armhole, this adjustment can be the most challenging.

For many sleeve styles, adjusting the depth of the armhole requires an equal adjustment to the sleeve. 

 For example, if you raise your armhole by 1 inch that would be 1 inch in front and 1 inch in back. You would then make your sleeve cap a total of 2" narrower (so the sleeve fits in the adjusted shortened armhole.

BUT: This adjustment is not easily accomplished with set in sleeve patterns.
 
To raise the armhole for set in sleeves:
  • Use a smaller size pattern
  • Substitute the smaller armhole depth from the smaller pattern
  • Knit the corresponding sleeve from the smaller patter
In other words, DO NOT adjust the armhole depth without re-charting the set in sleeve cap.
